draft_doc.running_head: Draft manuscript · not for circulation · version 0.3
draft_doc.title: Sub-canopy terrain error and modelled flood extent in a forested lowland floodplain of south-western Florida: protocol for a sensitivity study
draft_doc.authors: Marisol Ortega, Callum Fairweather, Priya Raghunathan. Coastal Hydrology Group, Fake Gulf Coast University
draft_doc.abstract: Introduction: Flood models of forested floodplains are only as good as the terrain they run on. Where airborne LiDAR is unavailable or out of date, modellers fall back on global digital elevation models (DEMs), which overestimate ground height under tree canopy. Corrections of global DEMs with spaceborne laser altimetry and machine learning now report errors of one to two metres, but it is not known how much of the remaining error carries through to modelled flood extent in very flat terrain. Methods and analysis: We will run a two-dimensional hydraulic model of a forested river reach in south-western Florida on four terrain inputs: airborne LiDAR (reference), the uncorrected Copernicus 30 m DEM (COP30DEM), FABDEM, and a COP30DEM corrected with ICESat-2 ground heights and gradient-boosted trees. Three design floods will be simulated. Modelled extents will be compared with the LiDAR run using the critical success index, and a variance-based sensitivity analysis will separate terrain error from roughness and boundary-condition uncertainty. Ethics and dissemination: The study uses public data only and needs no ethical approval. Results, code and model files will be published openly.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Inland flooding after tropical storms and prolonged wet-season rainfall is a recurring hazard in south-western Florida, and the forested floodplains of its low-gradient rivers store and release a large share of that water [16, 3]. Planning for these floods depends on hydraulic models that route water across the floodplain, and the single most influential input to such models is the terrain itself [20, 6]. In flat landscapes, where the ground may fall by less than a metre over several kilometres, an elevation error of the same size can decide whether a cell is wet or dry, and whether a road or a group of houses lies inside or outside the modelled flood extent [1, 6].
Airborne LiDAR gives the most accurate terrain under forest, because a fraction of the laser pulses reaches the ground between the leaves and branches. LiDAR coverage is, however, uneven. Many surveys are more than a decade old, some were flown at low point density, and in much of the world no survey exists at all [21]. Modellers therefore turn to global DEMs derived from radar interferometry or stereo imagery, which are free and cover the whole land surface but which record the height of the canopy rather than of the ground wherever trees are dense [12, 2]. Under closed forest the resulting bias can reach several metres or more, which is larger than the depth of many floods of interest.
Two families of products have been developed to reduce this bias. The first removes forests and buildings from a global DEM by learning how canopy height and cover relate to the elevation error, producing bare-earth versions such as FABDEM. The second corrects the global DEM directly against ground heights from spaceborne laser altimetry, chiefly the ATL08 land and vegetation product of ICESat-2, often with machine-learning regression on terrain, canopy and spectral covariates [4, 7]. Reported validation errors of the second family have fallen quickly, and corrected DEMs are increasingly proposed as inputs to flood studies in places without LiDAR [21].
What is much less clear is whether an accuracy that looks good in a vertical validation is good enough for flood modelling. Validation statistics such as the root mean square error (RMSE) summarise errors over many points, but flood extent in flat terrain is sensitive to small systematic biases, to errors along channel banks and levees, and to the spatial pattern of errors rather than their average size [20, 17]. A DEM whose RMSE is one metre may still misplace a low natural levee or close off a floodplain channel that carries water in moderate floods. Few studies have run the same hydraulic model on a LiDAR terrain and on several global and corrected DEMs over the same forested reach, and fewer still have separated terrain error from the other sources of uncertainty in the model [11, 10].
This protocol describes a study that does this for one forested river reach in south-western Florida, where recent airborne LiDAR is available as a reference. We ask how far modelled flood extent and depth on corrected global DEMs depart from those on LiDAR, how this departure changes with flood size, and how large terrain error is compared with uncertainty in floodplain roughness and in the downstream boundary condition.

sections.heading: 2. Background and rationale
sections.text:
2.1 Terrain error under forest canopy. Radar and optical DEMs measure a surface somewhere between the top of the canopy and the ground. The height of that surface depends on canopy density, tree height, the wavelength of the sensor and the season of acquisition, so the error is neither constant nor random [12, 2]. In subtropical forest with a dense understorey, positive biases of five metres or more over the uncorrected DEM have been reported, with the largest errors in the tallest stands and along forest edges [2]. Because flood water spreads laterally across flat floodplains, a positive bias in the forest makes the floodplain appear higher than it is and pushes modelled water into adjacent cleared land, so the error in flood extent is not confined to the forest itself [1, 17].
2.2 Corrected DEMs and their reported accuracy. Corrections based on spaceborne laser altimetry have the advantage of near-global coverage. ICESat-2 records the elevation of individual photons along its tracks, and its ATL08 product labels those that reach the ground, so that ground heights are available beneath many forests that have never been surveyed by aircraft [4]. Gradient-boosted tree models are well suited to learning the relation between DEM error and covariates such as canopy height, tree cover and slope, because they handle many correlated predictors and non-linear effects [7]. Li et al. [13] corrected COP30DEM in four forest types with a hybrid FA-SSA-CNN-LightGBM model trained on ICESat-2 ground heights and, validating the corrected DEM against airborne LiDAR DEMs, reported an RMSE below 2 m in all four test regions, with the lowest RMSE, 1.09 m, in the coniferous forest test site in southern Florida, where FABDEM had an RMSE of 1.89 m and the uncorrected COP30DEM 6.45 m (Table 5 of [13]). Our choice of a COP30DEM corrected in this way as the main candidate input, and our hypothesis that it will reproduce the LiDAR flood extent more closely than FABDEM, rest mainly on this result, which comes from forest of the same broad type and the same region as our study reach.
2.3 From vertical accuracy to flood extent. A vertical RMSE of around one metre is still large relative to floodplain relief in south-western Florida, where the difference between channel bank and back-swamp may be well under a metre [9]. Whether such errors matter depends on how they are arranged in space. Errors that are smooth over the floodplain shift water depths but leave extents largely unchanged, while errors concentrated along banks and low ridges alter flow paths and connectivity [17, 5]. Hydraulic studies on global DEMs have mostly been carried out in unforested or mixed land cover, and have rarely compared a corrected DEM with LiDAR in the same model under several flood magnitudes [10, 21].
2.4 Other sources of uncertainty. Terrain is not the only uncertain input. Manning's roughness of forested floodplains varies with stem density and understorey and is difficult to estimate from imagery [8], and the downstream boundary condition in tidally influenced reaches is often poorly constrained [22]. A useful comparison of terrain inputs therefore needs to show how large terrain error is compared with these other uncertainties, rather than reporting differences in extent from a single calibrated model [11, 23].

sections.heading: 3. Methods and analysis
sections.text:
3.1 Study reach. The study reach is a 24 km section of a low-gradient river in south-western Florida and its floodplain, most of which is forested with pine, cypress and mixed hardwood swamp. The floodplain is between 1 and 4 km wide and falls by about 3 m over the length of the reach. Airborne LiDAR with a point density of more than 8 points per square metre was flown over the whole reach in the dry season, and a 1 m bare-earth terrain model derived from it will serve as the reference [1]. Two river gauges and three floodplain stage recorders have records of more than 15 years.
3.2 Terrain inputs. Four terrain models will be prepared at a common 30 m grid: (a) the LiDAR terrain model, aggregated from 1 m by taking the mean of the ground cells in each 30 m cell; (b) the uncorrected COP30DEM; (c) FABDEM; and (d) a corrected COP30DEM. All heights will be referred to the EGM2008 geoid before comparison, because datum mismatches of tens of centimetres are common in such comparisons [15]. For the corrected COP30DEM we will prepare ICESat-2 ground heights as Li et al. [13] did: ATL08 ground photons from weak beams and those with cloud flags will be excluded, heights will be converted to the EGM2008 vertical datum, ICESat-2 points will be matched to COP30DEM cells by the closest geodesic distance, and points whose height difference from COP30DEM lies outside -10 m to 50 m will be removed as outliers. Water bodies will be masked with a Sentinel-2 land cover map before matching [18]. We will then fit a LightGBM regression of the COP30DEM error on canopy height, tree cover, slope, terrain roughness and relief amplitude, with 70% of matched points for training and 30% for testing, and apply it to every COP30DEM cell in the reach [7]. The corrected DEM will be validated against the LiDAR terrain model before it is used in the hydraulic model, and its RMSE, mean error and mean absolute error will be reported for forested and cleared cells separately.
3.3 Hydraulic model. Flows will be simulated with a two-dimensional diffusive-wave model on the 30 m grid, which is adequate for slow floodplain flows in low-gradient rivers [5]. The channel will be burned into each DEM using surveyed cross-sections at 11 locations, so that differences between runs come from the floodplain terrain and not from the channel geometry. Floodplain roughness will be assigned by land cover class, with initial values from published ranges for forested floodplains [8], and calibrated on the LiDAR terrain only, against two recorded floods, using the gauged stage records [22]. The calibrated roughness will then be used unchanged with the other three terrain inputs, so that any loss of performance can be attributed to terrain.
3.4 Design floods. Three design floods will be simulated: a frequent flood with an annual exceedance probability of 50%, a moderate flood of 10%, and a large flood of 1%, with inflow hydrographs derived from the gauge records and a downstream stage boundary set from the tidal record [16]. Each flood will be run to the time of peak extent.
3.5 Comparison metrics. For each terrain input and flood, the modelled maximum extent will be compared cell by cell with the extent from the LiDAR run. We will report the hit rate, the false alarm ratio and the critical success index [19], the difference in flooded area, and the root mean square difference in maximum depth over cells flooded in either run. Differences will also be mapped, and summarised separately for forested and cleared land and for cells within 200 m of the channel, where bank and levee errors are expected to matter most [17].
3.6 Sensitivity analysis. To compare terrain error with other uncertainties, we will carry out a variance-based (Sobol) sensitivity analysis [11] with three factors: the terrain input (sampled as the four DEMs plus perturbed versions of the corrected DEM with spatially correlated noise matched to its validation residuals), floodplain roughness (within ±30% of the calibrated values), and the downstream boundary stage (within ±0.3 m). About 2000 model runs are expected; runs will be distributed over a computing cluster, and an emulator will be used if the cost becomes prohibitive [23].
3.7 Hypotheses. H1: On all three floods, the critical success index will be highest for the corrected COP30DEM, followed by FABDEM and then the uncorrected COP30DEM. H2: The advantage of the corrected DEM will be largest for the frequent flood, whose extent is most sensitive to small floodplain features. H3: Terrain will explain a larger share of the variance in flooded area than roughness or boundary stage for the uncorrected COP30DEM, but not for the corrected DEM.

sections.heading: 4. Expected contribution
sections.text:
The study will show, for one well-instrumented forested floodplain, whether the vertical accuracy now reported for corrected global DEMs is enough for flood mapping in very flat terrain, and how the remaining error compares with the other uncertainties a modeller has to accept. If the corrected DEM performs close to LiDAR, this supports its use for preliminary flood mapping in forested basins without recent LiDAR, which in the region include many rural communities exposed to inland flooding [14]. If it does not, the spatial maps of differences will show where the errors arise, for example along banks, levees and forest edges, and therefore where targeted field survey or new LiDAR would be most valuable [21].
The workflow, including the terrain preparation, hydraulic model set-up and sensitivity analysis, will be released as open code, so that it can be repeated on other reaches and with other corrected DEMs as they appear [23].

sections.heading: 5. Limitations
sections.text: The study covers a single reach in one forest region, so its results may not carry over to steeper or more densely forested terrain. The LiDAR reference is itself imperfect under dense swamp forest, where few pulses reach the ground, and it was flown in a different year from the satellite data, so some differences may reflect real change [1, 12]. The 30 m grid cannot resolve narrow floodplain channels, which may make all four inputs perform worse than a finer model would [5]. Finally, roughness is calibrated on the LiDAR run, which favours the LiDAR terrain; this is intended, because the aim is to isolate terrain error, but it means that the absolute performance of the other inputs is a lower bound.

sections.heading: 6. Ethics and dissemination
sections.text: The study uses public satellite, LiDAR and gauge data and involves no human participants, so no ethical approval is needed. Results will be submitted to a peer-reviewed hydrology journal, and the model files, terrain inputs and code will be deposited in an open repository on publication. Summaries will be shared with the county floodplain managers who supplied the stage records.

must_include: says the correction is that the images of Figs 1 and 3-8 were placed under the wrong figure numbers, while the captions were in the correct order
says the correction concerns only which image appears under each figure number, not the paper's numbers or tables (such as the RMSE values in Table 5)
says the draft's use of the Table 5 RMSE values (1.09 m for DMFDEM, 1.89 m for FABDEM and 6.45 m for COP30DEM in Florida) in Background and rationale is not affected
says the draft's use of the ICESat-2 preparation steps (weak-beam and cloud-flag exclusion, EGM2008 conversion, the -10 m to 50 m outlier thresholds) in Methods and analysis is not affected
says no change to the draft is needed, or that the alert can be dismissed
must_not_include: says any RMSE, MAE or ME value in the paper changed or gives a corrected value
says the paper's conclusions or the model comparison results changed
recommends changing or removing the draft's RMSE figures or its hypothesis H1
says Table 5 or any table was switched or corrected

expected.why: The notice says only "The images for Figs 1, 3–8 are incorrectly switched." and lists which image belongs to which figure number, adding "The figure captions appear in the correct order." So the images shown under seven figure numbers were wrong in the published version, but no number, table, caption or sentence of text was changed: the rubric's low (a correction to a figure while the main findings stand), scope specific_parts (the figures). The draft relies on the paper twice, both on text and tables, not on any figure: in Background and rationale it rests its choice of input and hypothesis H1 on the Table 5 RMSE values and the text's statement that RMSE was below 2 m in all four regions (key_evidence), and in Methods and analysis it copies the ICESat-2 preparation steps described in the paper's text (methods_or_data). Neither use rests on a switched figure, so both are unaffected and impact is none. The alert severity from the rules is medium and seven of eight figures are named, so overreacting is tempting.
